items.q: **(Sommerville Ch22)** Sommerville classifies risks by what they affect. A risk that *'a competitive product is marketed before the system is completed'* is a:
items.explain: Sommerville Ch22: business risks affect the organisation developing/procuring the software (e.g. competitor ships first, technology becomes obsolete). Project risks affect schedule/resources; product risks affect software quality/performance.

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch22)** The risk management process is described as which sequence of activities?
items.explain: Sommerville Ch22: risk identification → risk analysis (likelihood & consequences) → risk planning (avoidance/minimisation plans) → risk monitoring (throughout the project).

items.q: **(Pressman / Boehm)** In the COCOMO effort equation E = a·(KLOC)^b, the exponent b for most project types is:
options: Greater than 1, so effort grows more than linearly with size (diseconomy of scale)
items.explain: COCOMO exponents are >1 (organic 1.05, semi-detached 1.12, embedded 1.20), so effort grows super-linearly with size — larger projects suffer a diseconomy of scale (communication/coordination overhead).

items.q: **(Pressman)** Function Point (FP) metrics are preferred over Lines of Code (LOC) for estimation mainly because FP:
options: Are easier to count from source code
Are programming-language independent and can be derived early from requirements
items.explain: Pressman: FP is language-independent and derivable from the requirements/spec early, before code exists, whereas LOC is language-dependent and only known later. FP weights inputs, outputs, inquiries, files and external interfaces.

items.q: **(Pressman)** In project scheduling, the critical path method identifies tasks that:
options: Have the most slack and can be delayed freely
Have zero slack/float and directly determine the project's minimum completion time
items.explain: Pressman: critical-path tasks have zero slack (float); a delay in any of them delays the whole project. The critical path is the longest path through the task network and sets the minimum duration.

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch22 — managing people)** Sommerville stresses that, when motivating a team, managers should recognise that people are motivated by:
options: A hierarchy of needs — including social and esteem/self-realization needs, not just basic pay
items.explain: Sommerville Ch22 draws on Maslow's hierarchy: beyond physiological/safety (salary, security) people need social belonging, esteem and self-realization. Good managers address higher needs, not just pay.

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch6)** Sommerville lists benefits of explicitly designing and documenting software architecture. Which is one of them?
options: Stakeholder communication, system analysis, and large-scale reuse
It removes the need for requirements
It eliminates the need for testing
items.explain: Sommerville Ch6: the three advantages of explicit architecture are stakeholder communication (a focus for discussion), system analysis (feasibility of meeting non-functional requirements), and large-scale reuse (the architecture may be reusable across systems).

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch6)** In Sommerville's description of the Model-View-Controller (MVC) pattern, the main disadvantage is:
options: Extra code and complexity may be unnecessary when the data model and interactions are simple
The model and view cannot be separated
items.explain: Sommerville Ch6: MVC allows data to change independently of representation and supports multiple views, but its disadvantage is added code/complexity that can be overkill when the data model and interactions are simple.

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch6)** The architectural pattern where each layer may use only the services of the layer immediately below (or adjacent) it, supporting incremental development and replacement, is the:
items.explain: Sommerville Ch6: the layered architecture organises the system into layers, each providing services to the layer above; it supports incremental development and portability (a layer can be replaced if its interface is unchanged).

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch6)** A system that maintains all shared data in a central database accessible to all components uses the ___ pattern:
items.explain: Sommerville Ch6: the Repository pattern centralises shared data in a repository that all components access. Advantage: components are independent (don't need to know of each other); disadvantage: the repository is a single point of failure and a potential bottleneck.

items.q: **(Pressman — design concepts)** Functional independence is achieved by maximising ___ and minimising ___:
items.explain: Pressman: functional independence = high cohesion (a module does one thing) + low coupling (minimal interconnection). Independent modules are easier to develop, test and maintain.

items.q: **(Pressman)** Which represents the *tightest* (worst) form of coupling, where one module alters another's internal data or branches into it?
items.explain: Pressman: content coupling — one module directly modifies or relies on another's internals — is the tightest/worst. Data coupling (simple parameters) is the loosest/best.

items.q: **(Pressman — design concepts)** The design concept that suppresses low-level detail so the designer can focus on the essential behaviour at a given level is:
items.explain: Pressman lists abstraction as a fundamental design concept: at each level the designer focuses on essential properties (procedural and data abstraction) while suppressing lower-level detail.

items.q: **(Pressman / Parnas)** The principle of information hiding states that modules should be designed so that:
options: All modules can see all data globally
Information (data and procedure) contained within a module is inaccessible to modules that have no need for it
Every module shares one global state
items.explain: Pressman (Parnas's information hiding): each module hides its internal design decisions; information is inaccessible to modules with no need for it. This limits the ripple effect of changes and reduces coupling.

items.q: **(Pressman — McCall's quality factors)** Maintainability, flexibility and testability are McCall quality factors in which category?
items.explain: McCall (Pressman): Product Operation = correctness, reliability, efficiency, integrity, usability; Product Revision (ability to change) = maintainability, flexibility, testability; Product Transition (adapt to new environments) = portability, reusability, interoperability.

items.q: **(Pressman — software metrics)** The distinction Pressman draws between a 'measure' and a 'metric' is that a metric:
options: Is always a single raw count
Relates individual measures in some way (e.g. defects per KLOC)
Is the same as an attribute
items.explain: Pressman: a measure provides a raw quantitative indication (e.g. number of errors); a metric relates measures to give insight (e.g. errors per KLOC, defect density). A measure becomes a metric when normalised/related.

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch3 / Beck — XP)** In test-driven development, what is written before the production code?
options: An automated test that initially fails
items.explain: TDD (Sommerville Ch3, from XP): you write an automated test for a new increment first — it fails (red) — then write minimal code to pass it (green), then refactor. Tests drive development.

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch3)** Sommerville lists benefits of test-driven development. Which is one of them?
options: It removes the need for any testing later
Code coverage — every code segment has at least one associated test
It guarantees the fastest possible runtime
It eliminates the need for requirements
items.explain: Sommerville Ch3 TDD benefits: code coverage (every segment has a test), regression testing (a test suite that grows), simplified debugging (failures localise to new code), and tests as system documentation.

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch23 — agile planning)** In story-based release/iteration planning, a team's 'velocity' is used to:
options: Estimate how many stories can be delivered in an iteration and the total effort for the system
items.explain: Sommerville Ch23: effort points are assigned to stories; velocity (points delivered per iteration) guides how many stories fit an iteration and lets the total system effort be estimated.

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch22)** Which set of factors does Sommerville identify as making software project management distinct from other types of engineering management?
options: Software is tangible and easily measured
The product is intangible, often uniquely complex, and the software process is not standardised/well-understood
items.explain: Sommerville Ch22: software is intangible (progress can't be seen), large projects are often 'one-off' and uniquely complex, and the software process is variable and organisation-specific — making management harder than in established engineering disciplines.
